lesson.menu_desc: Verbs followed by -ing or by to: what a contract clause asks you to do, to avoid and to refrain from, explained to a director
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- Doing or To Do
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Amanda Merlini | Lesson 11 -- Doing or To Do
lesson.grammar_point: verbs followed by gerund or infinitive

vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: to promise to do something and to keep doing it
to say that you do not agree with something or do not accept it
to try to get or to achieve something (formal)
to promise formally, often in a contract, to do something
to decide not to use a right or a rule that you have
to move an event or an action to a later date
to not do something because a rule or an agreement says so
to have the legal right to have or to do something

items.situation: Rafael asks: "What do they want us to do with the monitoring report?"
tips: They want us to deliver it within sixty days of each verification.

items.situation: He asks: "Can we sell the credits to somebody else in the meantime?"
tips: No. We have to refrain from selling them until the transfer is complete.

items.situation: He asks: "Should we sign now or wait?"
tips: I recommend signing now. Postponing it could cost us the buyer.

items.situation: He asks: "Did they accept our idea about the payment date?"
tips: Yes. They agreed to link the payment to the issuance.

items.situation: He asks: "What happens if we deliver late?"
tips: They would be entitled to terminate the agreement.
entitled to + verb: here to is part of the infinitive.

items.situation: He asks: "Will they accept a price review?"
tips: They may object to reviewing the price, so I suggest waiving it for the first year.

listenings.text: Hi Amanda, it is Ingrid, from the buyer's legal team. I promised to send the draft clause by Friday, and it is in your inbox now. Let me explain three points before you read it. First, my client has agreed to link the payment to the date the credits are issued, so we have stopped insisting on a calendar date. Second, we would like you to undertake to deliver a monitoring report within sixty days of each verification. We are not trying to control your project. We simply want to avoid paying for credits that nobody has checked. Third, and this is the sensitive one, the clause asks you to refrain from selling the same credits to anybody else until the transfer is complete. I expect your commercial team to object to that, and I am happy to discuss it. I suggest having a call on Tuesday. If Tuesday does not work, please let me know which day you prefer.

Most verbs in English take one pattern and keep it. You avoid doing something, and you agree to do something. But a few verbs change their meaning with the pattern, and in a legal document that change is a different fact. Take stop. We stopped negotiating means the negotiation ended. We stopped to negotiate means we interrupted something else in order to negotiate. Remember works the same way. I remember sending the notice is a memory about the past. I remembered to send the notice says something more useful: there was a duty, and I did not forget it. And then there is try. We tried to contact the verifier means we made an effort, and perhaps we failed. We tried contacting the verifier means it was one option among several. So my advice is simple. When stop, remember or try appears in a statement you are going to sign, read the sentence twice, and ask yourself which fact it states.

extra_audio.text: Start by saying which clause it is, and what it is about. Then say what we undertake to do. Then say what we must refrain from doing. Then say what the other side is entitled to do if we fail. And finally, give your recommendation.
